title: A Giant Rodent Roamed Thailand 34 Million Years Ago
summary:
Imagine a rodent the size of a medium dog, scurrying through a forest 34 million years ago. That is the picture painted by two fossil teeth found in a mine in southern Thailand. The teeth belonged to a previously unknown species called Yakamys sirindhornae, and they suggest giant rodents appeared earlier — and in more places — than scientists had thought.

The fossils were found at the Bang Mark Pit in the Krabi lignite mine in Thailand's Krabi Province. The team that identified them included scientists from McGill University, Thailand's Department of Mineral Resources, and French research organizations. The remains were just two teeth: a lower second molar and a lower incisor.

To estimate the animal's size, the researchers used seven established methods that calculate body mass from tooth measurements. Their best guess: the rodent weighed about 30 kilograms, roughly 66 pounds. That would make it about twice as heavy as other known rodents from the same period, including one called Hulgana.

Estimating a long-dead animal's weight from just two teeth involves a lot of uncertainty. Virginie Millien, a biology professor at McGill University and a co-author of the study, called it 'only a ballpark figure.' The limited fossils also make it hard to know how the animal lived or what it ate.

The name Yakamys combines 'yak,' the Thai word for giant, with 'mys,' the Greek word for mouse or rat. The second part of the name honors Princess Maha Chakri Sirindhorn, in recognition of her support for science and paleontological research in Thailand.

Until now, giant rodents were thought to have evolved mostly in South America. This discovery suggests Southeast Asia also played an important role in the early history of large-bodied rodents. More fossils may one day reveal how these ancient giants lived and how they relate to the huge rodents that appeared elsewhere in the world.
why_it_matters: The find rewrites the early story of giant rodents, showing Southeast Asia mattered as well as South America — and it shows how much history can hide in just two small teeth.

An incisor is one of the sharp front teeth, used for biting into food.
Lignite is a soft, brown kind of coal that forms from plants buried long ago.
Paleontological means to do with the study of ancient life through fossils.

background_read: A fossil is the preserved remains of a plant or animal that lived long ago, often just bones or teeth that survive after everything else has gone.
Rodents are mammals with strong front teeth for gnawing, and they include animals such as mice, rats, and squirrels.
Scientists can learn a lot from a single tooth: its size and shape can hint at how big the animal was and what it might have eaten.
This discovery matters because it changes where scientists think giant rodents first evolved, pointing to Southeast Asia as well as South America.
